title: The radial forearm flap as a sentinel flap in heart transplantation for early detection of rejection and protective immunomodulation
summary:
This study investigates a novel approach for monitoring rejection after heart transplantation. In addition to the donor heart, a small piece of skin tissue (radial forearm flap) is transplanted, serving as a so-called “sentinel flap.” Since skin is highly sensitive to immunological changes, this flap may detect early signs of rejection faster than current standard methods.

After transplantation, patients are monitored regularly. Small tissue samples are taken from the sentinel flap and analyzed. The aim is to enable earlier detection of rejection, improve treatment adjustments, and potentially reduce the need for invasive heart biopsies.

In addition, the study explores whether the sentinel flap itself may have a protective effect on the transplanted heart by positively influencing the immune response.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Indication for heart transplantation
Clinically stable condition following heart transplantation
Ability to understand the nature, significance, and implications of the study
Presence of controlled comorbidities (e.g., hypertension, diabetes mellitus) not expected to significantly affect immune response or study outcomes
Standard immunosuppressive therapy according to post–heart transplantation care is permitted
Exclusion criteria:
Known immunodeficiency or severe disorders of the immune system
Uncontrolled systemic infections or active inflammatory diseases
Severe additional organ failure significantly affecting postoperative outcomes
Advanced peripheral vascular disease (e.g., relevant atherosclerosis) with increased risk of flap failure
Participation in other experimental therapies within the last 6 months
Prior organ transplantation
Participation in clinical studies involving immunomodulatory or immunosuppressive interventions that may interfere with immune response assessment
